claims: Second-degree false imprisonment is generally a Class A misdemeanor or similar.
Second-degree false imprisonment is defined as knowingly restraining another person without legal authority or consent, substantially interfering with their liberty.
Second-degree false imprisonment does not require the use of force or fear.
Simply blocking an exit is sufficient for second-degree false imprisonment.
Second-degree false imprisonment is often treated as a misdemeanor with penalties up to one year in jail.
Second-degree false imprisonment may be a felony in certain scenarios involving minors.
Second-degree false imprisonment may be a felony under specific state laws like Pennsylvania.
In many jurisdictions, it is a defense if a business owner detained someone temporarily to investigate suspected shoplifting in a reasonable manner.
